theme: Nehemiah’s prayer; commissioned to rebuild the wall
readingInstruction: Read Nehemiah 1:1-2:20. Nehemiah, a cupbearer to the Persian king, hears that Jerusalem’s walls are still broken. Notice that he prays before he speaks, and speaks only after he has prayed for months.
settingTheScene: It is 445 BC, about thirteen years after Ezra. The temple stands, but Jerusalem has no walls, which leaves it defenseless and shameful. Nehemiah serves in the palace at Susa as cupbearer to Artaxerxes, a trusted position close to the king. A visitor from Judah brings him news of the city’s “great trouble and shame.” Nehemiah’s own memoir fills this book, and it is full of prayer.
observation: “When I heard these words I sat down and wept and mourned for days, and I continued fasting and praying before the God of heaven” (1:4).
“Let your ear be attentive and your eyes open, to hear the prayer of your servant” (1:6).
“Both I and my father’s house have sinned” (1:6).
“Remember the word that you commanded your servant Moses” (1:8).
“Then the king said to me, What are you requesting? So I prayed to the God of heaven” (2:4).
“And the king granted me what I asked, for the good hand of my God was upon me” (2:8).
“Let us rise up and build. So they strengthened their hands for the good work” (2:18).
“The God of heaven will make us prosper, and we his servants will arise and build” (2:20).
interpretation:
Nehemiah’s first response to bad news is tears and prayer. He does not rush to a plan. For about four months, from Chislev to Nisan, he fasts and prays. His prayer follows the pattern of Daniel 9 and Ezra 9: he praises God for his covenant love, confesses sins including his own and his father’s house, remembers the promise of Moses to gather the scattered, and asks for success before the king.

Then comes the moment. The king notices that his cupbearer is sad, which is dangerous, since sadness in the royal presence could cost a man his life. “Then I was very much afraid.” The king asks what he wants. Nehemiah does something wonderful: “So I prayed to the God of heaven.” In the span of a breath, between the king’s question and his own answer, he sends up a prayer. Then he answers boldly and specifically. He asks for time, letters of safe passage, and timber. All of it is given, “for the good hand of my God was upon me.”

Nehemiah arrives in Jerusalem and quietly inspects the walls at night. Only then does he tell the leaders about the vision God gave him. His appeal ties the work to what God has already done: “I told them how the hand of my God had been upon me for good.” They answer, “Let us rise up and build.”

Opposition appears at once, in the form of Sanballat, Tobiah, and Geshem, who mock and accuse. Nehemiah’s reply is calm: “The God of heaven will make us prosper.” He does not argue or defend himself. He states whose work it is.

The pattern is prayer, planning, and perseverance. Prayer came first and was sustained. Planning followed, with specific requests and a night survey. Then came bold action.
connection: Jesus told his disciples to pray and not lose heart (Luke 18:1). Philippians 4:6 says, “In everything by prayer and supplication with thanksgiving let your requests be made known to God.” James 1:5 promises wisdom to those who ask. Proverbs 21:1 says the king’s heart is a stream of water in the hand of the LORD. Colossians 4:2-3 asks us to continue steadfastly in prayer. Luke 14:28 teaches counting the cost before building.
application:
Practice the “arrow prayer” today: breathe a quick prayer before a hard conversation or decision.

Name a broken wall in your family, church, or community that burdens you. Pray about it for a week before you act.

Confess sins you share in, as Nehemiah did, and then ask God for his good hand.
prayerPrompts: Pray as Nehemiah did: praise God, confess your sin and your people’s, and name what burdens you.
Ask him to let his ear be attentive.
Tell him what you are asking him for.
